title: yo, te, lo, the rolled r, -ence → -encia

cards.title: yo = I (only for emphasis)
cards.body: Quiero already means 'I want', so Spanish normally leaves out the word for I. Yo is there for emphasis. In negatives the order is like English: yo no quiero.
cards.caveat: Not 'no yo quiero': no sits right before the verb.

cards.title: More -ation verbs
cards.body: Keep using the -ation → -ar route. Ilustrar contains luz, 'light' (z = s, or th in much of Spain).

cards.title: 'Find out' = inform myself
cards.body: Spanish says 'I want to find out' as 'I want to inform myself': me attaches to the verb.

cards.title: te = you (informal), block by block
cards.body: Te is informal 'you'. Like me, it attaches to the end of the verb. A sentence you think you can't say can often be built block by block: no quiero + obligar + te. Find the verb the long way: obligation → obligación → obligar.

examples.en: I don't want to oblige you (make you).
I don't want to provoke you.

cards.caveat: Obligar is everyday Spanish, closer to 'make (someone do something)'.

cards.title: lo = it
cards.body: Lo means 'it' and also joins the end of the verb.

cards.title: The rolled r
cards.body: An r at the start of a word, or a double rr, is rolled: a relaxed tongue lifted so the air flaps it. A tense mouth makes it harder. If you can't do it yet, don't force it; it often comes with listening. Some native speakers can't roll it either.

cards.title: Take the long route, slowly
cards.body: Don't jump straight from the English verb. Go participate → participation → participación → participar, syllable by syllable, so no extra sounds sneak in.

cards.title: experimentar: experiment and experience
cards.body: Experimentar means both 'to experiment' and 'to experience'. The nouns differ: experimento (experiment), experiencia (experience).

practice.en: I don't want to oblige you.
I don't want to provoke you.

practice.why: pero (single r) — perro, with rr, is dog.
